opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest shift is that AI will separate "work" from "labor." For a long time, a lot of what we call work has really been execution: writing boilerplate code, summarizing documents, filling in forms, tuning hyperparameters by trial and error. AI tools are getting very good at that layer. So the part of work that remains for people moves upward. It becomes about deciding what's worth doing, judging whether an output is actually right, and taking responsibility for the result.

In my own research I already see this. A few years ago, if I had an idea, it might take weeks of engineering to test it. Now I can prototype much faster with AI assistance, so the bottleneck is no longer "can I implement this," it's "is this the right question?" That sounds like good news, and in many ways it is, but it also raises the bar. If execution is cheap, then taste, insight, and the ability to define problems become what differentiates people.

There's a deeper implication too. For many people, work has provided structure, identity, and a sense of being needed. If AI takes over more and more of the routine parts, people may have to find meaning elsewhere, or redefine what meaningful work looks like for them. Some will love it, since they get to focus on creativity and exploration. Others may feel unmoored, because the skills they spent years building suddenly seem less valuable.

So I don't think the main question is whether there will still be jobs. It's how quickly individuals and institutions can adapt. Education, for example, still trains people mostly for execution. We need to train people to ask good questions, to work alongside these systems critically, and to keep learning continuously. And honestly, I also write novels in my spare time, partly because I think creative work that comes from your own experience is something people will value even more in a world where AI can produce a lot of competent content. In the end, AI may push us to rediscover why we work at all, not just to earn a living, but to express something that's uniquely ours.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI taking over routine tasks, but does not predict that large companies will need fewer employees or that everyone will become an entrepreneur or co-founder.

r002.rationale: It says people may need to find meaning elsewhere as routine work is automated, but does not connect this to companies needing fewer employees or to no longer being a component of a large organization.

r003.rationale: The response suggests rediscovering why people work, but does not liken this to a new Renaissance.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that AI tools are going to change what "work" even means, and we're only at the very beginning of that.

Let me start with what I see day to day. In research, a lot of what we used to spend time on was mechanical: writing boilerplate code, running sweeps, reading through dozens of papers to find the one relevant result, debugging a training run at two in the morning. Those things felt like work, and they consumed a huge fraction of our hours, but they were never the part that actually required a human. Now a model can do a first draft of most of that. So the time I spend shifts upward, toward deciding which question is worth asking, which experiment actually distinguishes between two hypotheses, and whether a result makes sense or whether the model is just confidently wrong. That last part matters more than ever.

I think that pattern generalizes. For a long time, a lot of jobs were valued because the person had acquired a skill that was expensive to acquire: knowing a programming language, knowing tax law, knowing how to write a persuasive memo. AI compresses the cost of acquiring and applying that kind of knowledge dramatically. What it doesn't compress nearly as well is judgment, taste, and the ability to understand what the real problem is. Those become the scarce resource. So the role of work moves away from "I am the person who can execute this" and toward "I am the person who knows what should be executed, and who can tell when the output is good."

There's a second shift that I think people underestimate. When one person can do what used to take a team, the unit of ambition changes. A single researcher can now explore ideas that would have needed five engineers and a year. A small group can build a product that used to need a company. That's exciting, but it also means the gap between people who learn to work with these tools and people who don't can widen very fast. I worry about that. The transition won't be smooth for everyone, and I don't think we should pretend otherwise.

The third thing, and maybe the most personal one, is the question of meaning. A lot of people derive identity from being good at something that was hard. If the hard thing becomes easy, that can feel like a loss, even if objectively you're more productive. I felt a version of this myself when I watched a model write code I would have been proud of a few years ago. My view is that the meaning doesn't disappear, it relocates. The craftsman who used to be proud of a perfect joint becomes proud of the whole piece of furniture. You're responsible for more, not less, and the satisfaction comes from the larger thing you can now make.

So if I had to summarize: AI tools will make work less about execution and more about direction, more about asking good questions and verifying answers. Routine labor shrinks. The leverage of any one person grows enormously. And the human parts of work, curiosity, judgment, and caring about whether the result is right, become the whole job rather than the small part at the top. Whether that's good or bad for a given person depends a lot on whether we help them make that transition, and I think that's the real challenge for the next decade.

r001.rationale: The response says individuals will gain leverage and small groups can build more, but it does not predict declining demand for large-company employees or that everyone will become an entrepreneur or co-founder.

r002.rationale: It discusses meaning shifting from mastery of a task to pride in a larger creation, but does not argue that people must find meaning beyond being part of a large organization.

r003.rationale: The response does not liken rediscovering one’s pursuits to a new Renaissance.

astra-6.text:
I think AI will change both what we do at work and why we work. Today, a lot of our time goes into executing tasks: writing code, gathering information, preparing documents. As AI takes on more of that, the human contribution may shift toward deciding which problems matter, asking the right questions, and judging whether the result is actually useful.

But that doesn’t automatically mean less work. If something becomes much cheaper to do, we often want to do more of it. You might build a product that previously required a whole team, or explore an idea that would have been too expensive to test. So there’s a possibility for people to become more independent and creative, although the transition could be difficult for people whose existing skills become less valuable.

There’s also a deeper question: work gives people more than income. It gives them structure, social connections, and a sense that they’re contributing. Even if AI makes us much more productive, we still need those things. So I think the challenge is not just how to automate tasks, but how to help people find meaningful ways to participate.

r001.rationale: It mentions people becoming more independent and creative, but does not predict that declining demand at large companies will push everyone toward entrepreneurship or co-founding.

r002.rationale: It says work provides structure, social connection, and contribution, and calls for meaningful participation. It does not connect this to companies needing fewer employees or finding meaning beyond membership in a large organization.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe discovering one’s own pursuits as a new Renaissance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI will change the relationship between effort and output. Today, a lot of our time goes into executing things: writing code, preparing documents, searching for information. As those tasks become easier, more of the value shifts toward deciding what to do, asking good questions, and judging whether the result actually makes sense.

But work is more than a way to produce things. It gives people income, structure, social connections, and a sense of achievement. Even if AI makes us much more productive, those needs don’t disappear. So the question is also how we organize society so that people can benefit from that productivity and still feel that they are contributing.

I’m optimistic that more people will be able to pursue ideas that previously required a large team or specialized skills. But that transition won’t be automatic. We’ll need to learn how to use these tools while continuing to develop our own judgment. When generating an answer becomes cheap, knowing which problems are worth solving becomes much more important.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI making tasks easier and enabling more people to pursue ideas, but does not predict declining demand for large-company employees or a shift toward entrepreneurship or co-founding.

r002.rationale: It says work provides income, structure, social connection, and achievement, and raises how people can continue contributing. It does not argue that companies will need fewer employees or that this will compel people to find meaning beyond roles in large organizations.

r003.rationale: The response does not liken rediscovering personal pursuits to a new Renaissance.
